cands.name: Kimberly Hardy

money.note: Individuals gave $378,648; PAC money $1,911; candidate's own money $0. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Social worker and professor of social work at Fayetteville State University since 2016. Ph.D. in social work from Morgan State University. Worked as a school social worker. Democratic nominee for NC House District 43 in 2020. Second Vice-Chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party since 2023. Has not held elected office.

endorsements.text: Ballotpedia lists Democrats Work for America among her 2026 endorsements and voter-guide recommendations. It also lists a number of informal "Sway" voting groups.

cands.gaps: We could not find where Kimberly Hardy was born or raised, or when she moved to North Carolina. We found no record of her holding elected or executive office. She has no documented actions in office on data centers, property taxes, land ownership, growth, immigration, policing, guns or school choice. We found no stated positions from her on those topics. Her campaign site covers jobs, environment, healthcare and education but does not address them. We found no statements from her on data centers or development. She did not complete Ballotpedia's 2026 candidate survey. Her only survey answers are from 2020 and were for a state House race.

qual.background: Career school social worker, then assistant professor of social work at the University of Connecticut (2010-13), the University of Saint Joseph (2013-16) and Fayetteville State University (2016 on). Lost the 2020 general election and 2022 primary for NC House District 43. Has held no elected or executive office.
qual.why: She has no governing experience in elected, executive, legal or staff roles, and her occupation (social work and teaching) is not directly tied to lawmaking. Her two earlier legislative bids were unsuccessful. Party office and nonprofit board service are not counted. Her policy exposure comes from social-work practice and research.

money.note: Individuals gave $957,967; PAC money $1,562,324; candidate's own money $0. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Republican U.S. representative for North Carolina's 7th District since 2015. Former state senator (2009–2013), aide to Sens. Jesse Helms and Elizabeth Dole, and USDA rural development official. Owner of The Rouzer Company. NC State graduate (1994).

controversies.text: Federal records show $27,900 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021; $16,590 from individuals passed through that PAC in 2025-26.
Missed 10 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (1.5%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 2, 2026-04-27 to 2026-04-27.

Rouzer said on Jan. 4, 2021 that he would object to several states' Electoral College votes. On Jan. 6 he joined 36 colleagues in a statement saying they would vote to sustain objections. They said the states changed election rules unconstitutionally and that they could not independently prove the fraud claims. State officials said they found no evidence of fraud that would change the result.

endorsements.text: Donald Trump (R) is listed as endorsing Rouzer in the 2026 race.

cands.gaps: We found no documented stance from Rouzer on data centers or on local development and growth. We also found nothing on homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign purchases of homes and land, H-1B visas, or teacher pay and school choice. We found no clear statement of when his family moved to North Carolina; the sources say only that he was raised in Durham. The campaign-site pages we could read date mostly from the 2016 and 2020 campaigns, so they may not reflect his current positions. The Ballotpedia page was cut off partway through the 118th Congress key votes, and its older sections, including the 2015-2017 votes, could not be read.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.
